newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi River shipping remains treacherous.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi River shipping remains treacherous.

text.p: Shipping remained treacherous on the lower Mississippi River on Thursday as rushing floodwaters made navigation difficult and contributed to another in a string of barge accidents, officials said.

A 195-foot barge was punctured by a tree in a fleeting area of the river near mile marker 227 at Baton Rouge before dawn Thursday, closing that section of the river for more than three hours, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
The barge, which was under tow, struck the tree while its tug was trying to ground the tow on the river bank to avoid a collision with another tug and tow, the Coast Guard said.
An undetermined amount of styrene leaked from a five-inch by three-inch gash in the 10,000 barrel capacity barge. The leak was plugged.
Crews were working to recover the spilled styrene from the river. The clear, insoluble and flammable liquid is hazardous to marine life in very low concentrations, the Coast Guard said.

At the mouth of the river in Southwest Pass tugs refloated the 799-foot Chemtrans Belocean (75,000 tonne dwt). The freighter grounded Tuesday with a cargo of coal, closing the river's deep-draft channel entrance of the river.
Shipping restrictions remained in place on sections of the river as swift currents following last week's crest make it difficult to navigate tows and deep-draft ships.

A number of restrictions in place, including a sharp cut in tugboat loads and daylight-only travel for some chemical and petrochemical-carrying vessels, as well as backed up traffic along the river, has cut the commercial traffic by more than half, according to shipping operators.

The Mississippi is one of the world's busiest waterways, with around one half billion tons of cargo traffic a year, according to the latest U.S. Army Corps of Engineers data. Around 17 percent of the total consists of oil and oil products, the figures show.
